nodes.text: Applying a lambda abstraction to an argument replaces x in t with u: (λx. t) u → t[x := u].
One use can connect separately to an argument and a work component.
A second use can likewise connect separately to an argument and a work component.
Two uses can share one intermediate share component.
The shared component can feed one argument.
An interaction step either removes an active pair or lets it pass through while reconnecting nearby wires.
Distinct active pairs never share an agent because each agent has one principal port.
Perfect confluence gives a one-step diamond: two possible steps from N reach a common net after one more interaction each.
Distinct active-pair rewrites commute because they use distinct agents and leave the same nearby wiring in either order.
Confluence and termination are separate: some nets reduce forever.
When a core interaction order normalizes, every normalizing order reaches the same result in the same number of interactions.
Earlier optimal-reduction nets used indexed fans and delimiter agents to track sharing scopes.
Δ-Nets replaces separate sharing-scope bookkeeping with a variable-arity replicator carrying a level and per-port deltas.
A Δ-Net core contains fans, erasers, and replicators.
A fan has exactly two auxiliary ports and represents lambda-term application and abstraction structure.
An eraser has no auxiliary ports and marks an unused bound variable.
A replicator has any natural-number auxiliary arity and joins uses of one shared value.
A replicator level names its sharing context, while each auxiliary port delta adjusts a replica's level when it exits that port.
ΔL permits fans only; ΔA adds erasers; ΔI adds replicators; ΔK permits all three agents.
Linear terms have exactly one bound use, affine terms at most one, relevant terms at least one, and full terms any count.
Equal replicators formally require matching level, arity, and every port delta.
For well-formed nets translated from lambda terms, active replicators at the same level are already equal.
Annihilation removes equal agents and reconnects corresponding auxiliary ports.
Erasure deletes the distinct agent met by an eraser because the eraser has no auxiliary ports.
Distinct non-eraser agents commute, producing outgoing copies according to the other agent's auxiliary-port count.
Fan annihilation is beta-reduction in graph form.
When a replicator meets a fan, the replicator is copied through the fan's two auxiliary ports and the fan is copied through every replicator port.
Fan-replicator reconnection is determined by port identities: (Fᵢ)ⱼ ↔ (Rʲ)ᵢ.
Equal replicators annihilate only when level, arity, and every port delta match; same level suffices for well-formed lambda translations.
Replicators at different levels commute rather than annihilate.
When lower-level R meets higher-level H, R creates one H replica per R auxiliary port.
Each H replica's new level equals H's old level plus the delta on the R port it exits.
H creates one exact copy of R per H auxiliary port; those R copies preserve R's level and deltas.
During different-level replicator commutation, auxiliary port j of each H replica connects to the matching port of Rʲ.
A port delta is an integer local level adjustment applied to every higher-level replica exiting through that port.
For R at level 2, an endpoint at level 2 gives delta 0 and an endpoint at level 5 gives delta +3.
An H replica at level 7 exits through delta 0 at level 7 and through delta +3 at level 10.
A delta may be negative, zero, or positive.
For each lambda fragment, the translation φ is a bijection between terms and canonical Δ-Nets.
The translation is inductive: translate smaller term fragments first and then wire them into larger fragments.
Every translated fragment has one incoming wire and zero or more outgoing wires; the outer net has one root.
A free variable becomes a named boundary node rather than a rewriting agent.
A bound variable occurrence is a wire whose endpoint later connects to its owning binder directly or through a sharing replicator.
An abstraction fan connects its first auxiliary port to the body and its second auxiliary port to the bound variable.
An unused bound variable connects the abstraction's variable port to an eraser in ΔA and ΔK.
A one-port replicator with zero delta is equivalent to a wire and is omitted from canonical construction.
An abstraction's bound-variable port connects directly to one occurrence, to an eraser when unused, or to a replicator when several occurrences share one value.
An application fan connects its principal port to the function, first auxiliary port to the result, and second auxiliary port to the argument.
For an application [M N] at level ℓ, M has level ℓ and N has level ℓ + 1.
For an abstraction λx.M at level ℓ, its body M remains at level ℓ and a needed sharing replicator Rₓ has level ℓ + 1.
The whole translated term begins at level 0.
A bound occurrence's wire endpoint has the level reached by walking the source syntax to that occurrence.
Walking a lambda body or an application function preserves the current level; entering an application argument adds one.
A replicator port delta equals its connected occurrence level minus the replicator level.
For λx. x (g x), the two x occurrences have levels 0 and 2, while Rₓ has level 1 and deltas ⟨−1, +1⟩.
The linear term (λx.x)(λy.y) reduces by one fan annihilation to λy.y.
The term λx.x x uses a two-port replicator because one bound input has two consumers.
For [λx.x x]₀, the replicator has level 1, with function-use delta −1 and argument-use delta 0.
A level delta is neither a copy count nor a source-level variable value; it records relative sharing context at a consumer.
For λx. x (x (x x)), the binder replicator is at level 1 and its four occurrence deltas are ⟨−1, 0, +1, +2⟩.
The four occurrence endpoint levels in λx. x (x (x x)) are 0, 1, 2, and 3.
Applying λx. x (x (x x)) to N produces N (N (N N)) by beta-reduction.
Translation produces canonical nets, while proper nets are intermediate nets reachable by zero or more Δ interactions.
Canonicalization restores a proper net to the canonical shape expected by back-translation.
In ΔA and ΔK, erasure canonicalization marks nodes reachable from the root and deletes unmarked material.
When deleting unreachable material leaves an exposed connection in the net, that connection is terminated by an eraser.
The erasure sweep may run at the end or earlier to save space; the paper recommends sweeping after applications of abstractions that ignore their arguments when memory matters most.
In ΔI and ΔK, consecutive replicators can merge when a local level test proves the later replicator is unpaired.
For consecutive replicators A and B joined through delta d, B is known unpaired when 0 ≤ lB − lA ≤ d.
Replicator merging preserves external endpoint levels while recomputing deltas relative to the surviving replicator's level.
In ΔK, unpaired replicator ports leading directly to erasers can be removed.
A remaining one-port unpaired replicator with delta zero collapses to a wire.
Canonicalization needs a schedule because it can touch ports that are not principal-to-principal active pairs.
The prescribed nonlinear-system schedule selects an outermost reducible pattern and then the leftmost candidate.
A reducible pair may run early when it will eventually reach leftmost-outermost position unchanged.
The full algorithm translates a term with φ, reduces through proper nets, normalizes and canonicalizes with Ω, then reads back with φ⁻¹.
Leftmost-outermost reduction avoids evaluating subnets that will later be erased.
Replicators represent shared use in the graph, avoiding repeated evaluation solely because an expression has multiple consumers.
Perfect confluence permits disjoint active pairs to choose and apply local interaction rules independently.
In ΔL, every proper net is canonical and n beta-reductions correspond to n interactions in any order.
ΔA requires erasure canonicalization; ΔI requires replicator merging; ΔK requires erasure, merge, and decay canonicalizations.
The three-agent interaction core has the one-step diamond property.
For nonlinear systems, the paper claims Church-Rosser confluence and optimality only after adding canonicalization and a global schedule.
Δ-Nets aims to represent each sharing context with a variable-arity replicator while using local interactions and limited global discipline to avoid preventable work.
